name: The king in the endgame
goal: Once the queens have been traded, you can bring your king into the game to attack pawns and support your own.
intro: While there are still many pieces on the board, your king hides behind its pawns. Once the queens are traded, it is safe to bring the king out, and it becomes a strong piece. An active king can walk up the board to win pawns the enemy king cannot defend, and it can walk beside your own pawn to lead it to promotion. In endgames with only kings and pawns left, the side whose king gets there first usually wins.

parts.title: Pawns on both sides
parts.keyIdea: Take your king to the side of the board where the enemy king is not, and win the pawns it cannot protect.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White, and only kings and pawns are left. Black's king is on the queenside (the a- to d-files), close to its own pawns there. Which black pawn can that king not protect in time?

notes.text: Kg4, the king to g4, sets off for the pawn on h6. Your king needs three moves to take it, and Black's king needs three moves to reach g7 and guard it, but you move first.
One more step. Black's king is hurrying over, but it is one move too slow.

The pawn falls, and the pawns are level: four each. Your king is now active on the kingside (the e- to h-files), while Black's king has left its queenside pawns behind, and the Engine judges that you are winning.

parts.title: Black's pawns have moved up
parts.keyIdea: Walk your king into the enemy's half of the board through squares no enemy pawn can attack, and hit the pawns from behind.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White, and only kings and pawns are left. On the queenside the pawns block each other and cannot move. Black's kingside pawns have moved forward, leaving squares behind them that no black pawn can ever guard. Find a path for your king into Black's position.
parts.line: Ke4 Kd6 Kf5 Ke7 Kg6 e4 fxe4 Ke6 Kxh6

notes.text: Ke4, the king to e4, heads for the kingside, where Black's pawns are. Black's king, on c6, is further away from them than yours.
No black pawn can ever attack f5, so your king is safe there, right in front of Black's pawns. Black's king has to come back to guard the f6 pawn.
Your king slips round to g6, behind Black's pawns, and attacks the pawn on h6. Black's king cannot defend it: every empty square next to h6 is also next to your king.
Black pushed the e-pawn to e4, attacking your pawn on f3. If Black took it, the new black pawn on f3 would have a clear run to promotion, so your f-pawn takes first, and you are a pawn up.
Black's king came back to e6, but it is too far away to help on the kingside. Your king takes the h6 pawn from behind, and you are two pawns up.

parts.title: A pawn and its king
parts.keyIdea: Put your king beside your pawn's path to promotion, so the enemy king cannot get in front of the pawn.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Your g-pawn wants to reach g8, but Black's king on f8 is close by, and Black's b-pawn is ready to run as well. Your king can help your pawn.
parts.line: Kh7 Ke7 g6 b4 g7 b3 g8=Q

notes.text: Kh7, the king to h7, takes g7 and g8 away from Black's king, so nothing can stop the g-pawn now. If you had pushed g6 at once, Black's king would have stepped to g8, right in front of the pawn, and the pawn would be stuck.
Now the pawn walks forward, and your king guards every square in front of it.
Black's b-pawn is racing too, but yours is well ahead: after this move it needs one more step, and Black's pawn on b4 still needs three.
The pawn promotes to a queen. With a queen against Black's lone pawn, you are winning.
